Full_Text: Since 2007, sperm and egg donation in Finland has not been anonymous. The first children conceived since then are reaching adulthood, granting them the right to learn the identity of their donor. In Finland, it has for several years no longer been possible to donate gametes anonymously. The Act on Assisted Fertility Treatments, which entered into force in September 2007, requires that all donors be registered in a database maintained by the Finnish Supervisory Agency. The register contains the donor's first and last name, date of birth and nationality. Even before 2007, donors could consent to having their details recorded, but back then, it was voluntary. The first children conceived under the current regulatory framework will turn 18 this year. According to the Finnish Institute for Health and Welfare (THL), 402 children were born as a result of treatments using donated gametes in 2007. Antti Perheentupa, a reproductive medicine expert at Turku University Hospital, said that the reform initially caused widespread concern within the field. "We thought that no one would want to become a donor anymore. For a time, the number of donors did drop, but when we spoke publicly in the media about the problem, the situation improved," he said According to Perheentupa, the rationale for banning anonymous donation was that children conceived this way should have the right to know about their genetic background and biological origins. Perheentupa said it is difficult to estimate how many will choose to exercise the right to find out the identity of their donor. Today, around 800 children are born in Finland each year with the help of donated sperm and egg cells.

Headline: News
Full_Text: Misuse can quickly cause permanent harm, Fimea says. Finland's medicines agency (Fimea) is warning about social media challenges involving over-the-counter drugs, as the consequences can be life threatening. Some challenges circulating on social media have involved paracetamol and acetylsalicylic acid. Paracetamol, commonly used for pain relief and fever reduction, is safe when taken in the correct dose, but even a slight overdose can cause serious liver damage, Fimea said in a statement. Acetylsalicylic acid, commonly known as aspirin, also has blood-thinning properties. "High doses or prolonged use of acetylsalicylic acid can cause stomach and intestinal problems, and in some cases potentially life-threatening gastrointestinal bleeding," said Piia Vuorela, a director at Fimea. She said that adults should talk with children and teens about the social media challenges and the risks associated with medicines. Yle News' All Points North podcast looked at moves to ban social media for kids in Finland.

Headline: News
Full_Text: Rescuers located the victims using tracking devices, but they were already dead. Two Finns, between the ages of 50 and 60, have died in an avalanche in northern Italy, according to Italian public broadcaster RAI. The accident occurred on Thursday afternoon near the Solda ski resort in South Tyrol, close to the Swiss border. The victims were backcountry skiers, according to RAI. One other Finnish skier survived. Helicopter-bound rescuers, en route to a separate avalanche, spotted someone digging in the snow and used beacons to locate the victims, who were found dead. One victim was found 60 centimetres beneath the snow, the other 1.5 metres deep. Avalanches are common in the area, RAI noted. The Finnish Foreign Ministry has confirmed the incident.

Headline: News
Full_Text: Finland will admit 50 Venezuelans from Peru as part of its annual refugee quota. The government has confirmed its 2026 refugee quota, keeping it unchanged from the past two years. Finland admits 500 quota refugees annually. This year, that figure includes 150 Afghans from Iran, 120 Congolese from Rwanda and 100 Syrians from Turkey. In addition, Finland will admit 50 Venezuelans from Peru, 30 evacuees from Libya via Rwanda, and 50 emergency cases without nationality or regional restrictions. Last year's quota distribution sparked debate in Finland after the Non-Discrimination Ombudsman suggested the Interior Ministry's political leadership was prioritising Christian asylum seekers. The Chancellor of Justice ultimately found the preparation of the allocation flawed but determined that religion had not been used unlawfully as a criterion.

Headline: News
Full_Text: Even as gold retreats from record highs, Finns continue cashing in on the precious metal. In an interview with Helsingin Sanomat, EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said Europe should begin a discussion about developing its own nuclear deterrent. She argued that nuclear deterrence could feature in future debates, given the current security environment and the reality that nuclear weapons remain the only effective deterrent. At the same time, HS noted, Kallas spoke cautiously and stressed the risks associated with nuclear proliferation. Within Europe, only France and Britain have nuclear weapons, while several countries are bound by treaties aimed at limiting their spread. Kallas, a former Estonian prime minister, was in Finland on Thursday. An explosion struck a cargo ship, MSC Giada III bound for St Petersburg in the Gulf of Finland on Wednesday, reports Ilta-Sanomat, citing The Moscow Times and the investigative site Insider. The Liberian-flagged vessel was travelling from Antwerp to St Petersburg and carried a crew of 22. The captain is Russian, while the rest of the crew are from Myanmar. Ukrainian outlet United24 claims the MSC Giada III forms part of Russia's so-called shadow fleet. These are ageing vessels often sailing under flags of convenience and used to circumvent Western sanctions. The ship had reportedly been observed earlier this year close to the Turkish coast in the Black Sea. Vans touring Finland to buy scrap gold are an increasingly common sight, even in small towns. Markus Rasimus, Lapland regional manager at Suomen Kultareservi, told Maaseudun Tulevaisuus that supplies show little sign of drying up, with sellers offering up everything from dental gold to bullion. Gold prices, which have risen steadily, briefly hit a record $5,600 an ounce last Thursday before falling 12 percent the following day. Typical sellers are women over 50, though younger people — often cashing in inherited jewellery — are also active. Individual transactions now commonly fetch 1,500–3,000 euros, as fewer young Finns choose to wear gold jewellery, preferring the cash instead.

Headline: News
Full_Text: Finland appears in US State Department cables on Greenlan, obtained by Politico. Finland features in US State Department dispatches obtained by Politico which relate to Greenland. "The Finns were desperate to prevent a trade war over the island," Politico wrote of diplomatic exchanges in the aftermath of Donald Trump's demands to acquire Greenland. According to Politico, Finnish Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen (NCP) told visiting members of the United States Congress that the deployment of a few Finnish soldiers to Greenland had been a "misunderstanding." The claim appears in a diplomatic cable sent from the US embassy in Helsinki on 20 January. The foreign ministry has rejected this account, saying Finland's dispatch of officers to Greenland was not the result of any misunderstanding. In January, Finland said it would send two liaison officers to Greenland to explore training opportunities. The announcement came just days after the White House had indicated that the United States was also considering military options related to Greenland. According to the online publication, Valtonen came across as eager to calm tensions. It cited Valtonen as saying Finland had no plans of any kind to do anything "against the Americans," adding that "a couple of guys", referring to the Finnish officers in Greenland, had already returned to Finland. Politico also suggested Valtonen downplayed the European Union's threat of retaliatory tariffs, describing it as a "negotiating tactic" and said she intended to press the bloc to "do anything to prevent a trade war." "Let's not get a divorce," Valtonen said, according to one cable, "especially not a messy one." In mid-January, Trump threatened to impose tariffs on countries that refused to comply with his demand concerning Greenland. Politico said the Finnish leadership did not respond to a request for comment. The cables exposed by Politico also highlight China's apparent hope that Trump's demand would drive a wedge between Europe and the United States. Politico noted that the exchanges, more than anything, underscore how important the US remains to Europe.

Headline: News
Full_Text: Regularly scheduled maintenance went wrong on Sunday morning, as services were to have come back online. The bank said in the afternoon that services were "being brought back into use gradually". One of Finland’s biggest banking groups, Nordea, apologised to customers on Sunday as planned maintenance work dragged on longer than expected due to an "unexpected technical fault". After 3pm, the bank said it had the maintenance work and that services were "being brought back into use gradually". Services were originally supposed to be returned to normal as of 9am, but still persisted into the afternoon. Nordea said in the morning that the problem had been "localised" and that services would be restored as soon as possible. However it did not indicate when operations might return to normal. The Downdetector service, which tracks online glitches, showed a spike in Finnish Nordea outage reports on Sunday morning, followed by another peak in the early afternoon. After 3pm, the number of reports dropped. In the meantime, Nordea said some services were "functioning in a limited capacity". It warned of occasional interruptions in card payments, and said that cash withdrawals should work via the checkouts at K grocery shops, Tokmanni discount stores and R-kiosks. The bank apologised for the inconvenience caused to customers due to the open-ended extension of maintenance work. 3.25pm: Updated with announcement of restoration of services.

Headline: News
Full_Text: The financial group said it is able to redeem the funds due to glimpses of recovery in the real estate market. OP Pohjola is opening two of its real estate funds for redemption, according to the Finnish financial giant. Many small-time investors have been waiting for such an announcement, as the bank had suspended investor cash-outs of real estate funds more than a year ago, due to weak sales in the sector. OP was among a number of banks that suspended redemptions of real estate funds. According to OP, it is now able to redeem the funds due to glimpses of recovery in the real estate market. OP said that its Public Services Real Estate Fund and Rental Yield Fund would be opened for redemption on Tuesday. "We see that the real estate market situation has now stabilised to the point where we can start fund subscriptions and redemptions," OP said in a press release.

Headline: News
Full_Text: The corporate giants told Yle they are not making comments ahead of releasing their financial results. Five of Finland's six biggest listed companies replied to Yle regarding US President Donald Trump's latest tariff threats. Among the Finnish firms that responded were Kone, Wärtsilä, UPM-Kymmene and Valmet, all of which count the United States as an important export market. None was prepared to speculate. Each declined to comment, citing the quiet period, a convention under which listed companies refrain from discussing financial performance, markets or prospects in the 30 days before publishing results. The American president has warned of an additional 10 percent levy on imports from eight European countries should he fail to secure Greenland, either by purchase or by force. In addition to Finland, these countries are Denmark, Sweden, Norway, Germany, France, the Netherlands and Britain. So far, the US Supreme Court has yet to rule on the legality of Trump's proposed increases in import tariffs.

Headline: News
Full_Text: Bankruptcy filings are up across nearly all sectors, according to Statistics Finland. The number of bankruptcies in Finland has continued to rise for the past three years, new data shows. According to Statistics Finland, just over 3,900 companies filed for bankruptcy last year — the largest figure seen since 1996, which came after years of a serious economic crisis. Last year's bankrupt companies employed around 14,300 people. StatFin reported that 360 bankruptcy proceedings were initiated in December 2025, or 92 more than the same month the previous year — a 34 percent increase. The number-crunching agency said that the recent larger wave of bankruptcies began a few years ago. An average of 3,600 companies have filed for bankruptcy annually since 2023. The yearly average during the 2010s was around 2,700 companies. According to the agency's senior statistician, Mira Kuussaari, last year's annual bankruptcy figure has been higher just three times during the 2000s: during the global financial crisis of 2009, in 2013 and then in 2023, when the current wave of bankruptcies began. However, the number of employees affected by companies going bust suggests that it is mostly SMEs that are being affected, on average, she explained. The agency reported that the largest number of firms filing for bankruptcy were in the construction sector — a total of 768. However, according to Kuusisari, the number of construction companies filing for bankruptcy peaked in 2023. "In practically all other sectors, the trend has been upward," she said in a press release.

Headline: News
Full_Text: The prospective buyers include US petroleum company Chevron and private equity firm Quantum Capital Group, according to the Financial Times. US petroleum company Chevron and the private equity firm Quantum Capital Group plan to buy the international assets of Lukoil, the sanctioned Russian oil company, according to the Financial Times. If the deal goes through, the two companies aim to share the assets, which are said to be valued at around 22 billion US dollars, the UK-based business paper said, citing unspecified sources. It reported that Quantum was leading the bidding process for Lukoil's gas and oil production, refineries and more than 2,000 petrol stations across Europe, Asia and the Middle East. That deal would also include Lukoil's petrol station chain Teboil, which until fairly recently continued to operate across Finland. However, Teboil announced that it was shutting down its operations in Finland in November, following the difficulties caused by US sanctions against Russian oil companies, including Lukoil and Rosneft, in October. According to FT, the US Treasury Department has given the companies until January 17 to negotiate the deal, which also requires the approval of US President Donald Trump. The business paper noted that American equity firm Carlyle Group and Dubai-based investment outfit International Holding Company were also bidding on Lukoil.

Headline: News
Full_Text: In a survey, a fifth of respondents said they consciously take a break from alcohol consumption at one or more points during the year. Sales of non-alcoholic beverages have risen at a record pace in Finland, the state alcohol monopoly Alko said on Friday. Alko sold over 850,000 litres of non-alcoholic beverages last year, an increase of 40 percent from the year before. About a decade ago, the firm sold approximately 186,000 litres of non-alcoholic beverages annually — meaning there has been a five-fold increase in sales over the past 10 years. Worldwide, the non-alcoholic beverage market grew by approximately nine percent last year, Alko noted in a press release. "We are constantly striving to introduce new, interesting non-alcoholic alternatives alongside traditional alcoholic beverages, as is well suited to Alko's core mission of preventing alcohol-related harm," Product Group Manager Mika Kauppinen said in the statement. Alko was set up by the Finnish state in 1932. It was given the exclusive right to import, export, manufacture and sell alcoholic beverages after Finland's period of prohibition was repealed. In a survey commissioned by Alko, a fifth of respondents said they consciously take a break from alcohol consumption at one or more points during the year. Nearly half of respondents said that alcohol impairs the quality of their sleep, while almost one-third said they want to reduce their consumption in general. Customers said they particularly choose non-alcoholic drinks when attending a party but planning to drive (64%), taking a sauna (40%) or relaxing at home (31%). About 700 people responded to the survey last month. A new tax on alcohol that took effect on New Year's Day raised the price of a bottle of beer by a few cents and a bottle of wine by around 50 cents.

Headline: News
Full_Text: Can you retire if you've never worked? A striking number of young people in Finland are applying for disability pensions before they have even entered working life, reports Helsingin Sanomat. That's according to the findings of a study published in a report by public sector pension insurer Keva. According to the report, only about 20 percent of under-30s who applied for a disability pension or vocational rehabilitation on mental health grounds had actually been employed before submitting their application. Mental health problems are the leading reason for seeking disability pensions and earnings-related rehabilitation in Finland's public sector. Kauppalehti explains how a weather phenomenon is driving up the price of spot electricity in Finland. In many areas, ice has built up on turbine blades at wind farms. Combined with weak winds, the situation has slashed output from the country's wind fleet. Forecasts suggest conditions will deteriorate further on Wednesday. On Tuesday, spot prices climbed to nearly 40 cents per kilowatt-hour. Icing on turbines is a routine winter hazard in Nordic countries, but its severity this season has been worse than in previous years. Blade heating systems can mitigate the problem, but the responsibility for such measures has largely been left to the wind power industry itself. More and more Finns are looking for alternatives to Gmail and other American digital services, according to Hufvudstadsbladet. According to Petteri Järvinen, an IT expert who has been sounding the alarm over US tech dependence, it is time to abandon the idea that email should be free. "Stop being stingy," he told the daily, suggesting that users should be prepared to pay a few euros a month for an email account. "If we are not willing to pay, we will inevitably end up in the laps of Google or Microsoft. If we want European alternatives, we must be ready to pay a few euros per month." People pay for bus tickets and countless other services, Järvinen noted, so why should email be an exception?

Headline: News
Full_Text: As the housing market slowed, many of the small-time investors wanted to sell off their shares — but due to sluggish real estate sales, there were not enough funds to honour the redemptions. More than 6,000 Ålandsbanken customers who invested in real estate funds will need to wait even longer to cash out, according to Ålands Radio. The news outlet reports that the bank informed customers about the situation on Friday, telling them it would take at least another fiscal quarter before they would be able to access their funds. One of the thousands of affected investors, Karola Molander, told the news outlet that the bank was now telling dissatisfied customers to contact its complaints department by mail, or to reach out to the Finnish Financial Ombudsman Bureau (Fine). An Yle News article in November explained that many small-time investors had a rude awakening when they realised that they could not redeem their holdings in almost a dozen real estate funds. As the housing market slowed, many investors wanted to sell off their shares — but due to sluggish real estate sales, there were not enough funds to honour the customers' redemptions. While Ålandsbanken investors were the first to be impacted in 2023, tens of thousands of customers at other banks, including OP Bank, were similarly affected. According to Ålands Radio, Ålandsbanken's fund manager Carola Nilsson, is scheduled to comment about the matter on Ålands Radio later on Monday.

Headline: News
Full_Text: There were over a quarter of a million people out of work in Finland in November last year, or 10.6 percent of the workforce. Finland's unemployment rate is statistically the worst in the European Union, according to figures published on Thursday by Eurostat, the European Commission’s data-crunching agency. The stats show that there were over a quarter of a million people out of work in Finland in November, representing 10.6 percent of the workforce. This rate is higher than that of Spain, which previously held the unwanted top spot in the EU's unemployment charts. The bleak situation marks Finland's highest unemployment rate since the aftermath of the global financial crisis in 2009, and reflects the poor state of the Finnish economy compared to other EU member states. As a point of comparison, the unemployment rate in the Netherlands in November was just 4 percent, while the EU average was 6 percent. The long-term trends also reveal that countries in southern parts of Europe which have traditionally had stubbornly high unemployment rates — such as Spain and Greece — have significantly improved their situations over the past decade. At the same time, Finland's trend — and that of Sweden too — has moved in the opposite direction. Finland's rising unemployment rate can be at least partly explained by the fact that the country's labour force has grown, in particular because of increased numbers of people moving to Finland from abroad in recent years. However, their arrival has coincided with a downturn in the Finnish economy and increased difficulty in finding work. In addition, Finland's government has introduced a number of measures which have been criticised by immigrant associations as making life more difficult for newcomers. However, despite the latest unemployment figures from Eurostat, Finland's Ministry of Economic Affairs and Employment has argued that the situation will improve during the coming 12 months. In a statement, the ministry noted that the number of people in employment in Finland has increased by about 25,000 over the past year, and more positions are becoming available in certain sectors.

Headline: News
Full_Text: According to Seta, the proportion of what it refers to as "rainbow youth" who were targeted by school bullying – including harassment, discrimination and violence – rose slightly between 2023 and last year. Bullying of LGBTQ+ youth at Finland’s school has increased, says Seta, the country’s main NGO representing members of sexual and gender minorities. In a press release on Monday, the human rights group cited the latest school health survey published by Finland's public health authority THL, which shows few changes in the wellbeing of 8th and 9th grade LGBTQ+ youth between 2019 and 2025. According to Seta, the proportion of what it refers to as "rainbow youth" who were targeted by school bullying – including harassment, discrimination and violence – rose slightly between 2023 and last year. Some 22 percent of 8th and 9th graders belonging to gender minorities and 16 percent of those belonging to sexual minorities reported that they had been bullied at school at least once a week during the school year. In response, Seta has called for targeted actions to improve the well-being of children and youth who belong to sexual and gender minorities. As measured in the School Health Survey published in late January, young people belonging to these groups experienced all forms of school bullying at two to three times the rate of other young people. The most common experiences were name-calling and shaming, facial expressions and gestures, spreading of lies and offensive language, as well as exclusion. "It is truly alarming that rainbow youth's experiences of harassment, discrimination and violence in schools have become even more common," Seta youth work advocacy expert Teija Ryhtä said in the statement. Ryhtä pointed out that bullying can also be life-threatening, while at the same time, hate speech, discrimination and harassment have become more prevalent in Finnish society in general in recent years. Seta also points to a more positive trend in the THL study: a slight decrease in reported experiences of loneliness among LGBTQ+ youth between 2023 and last, as well as gradual improvement in general life satisfaction. Last year, 46 percent of sexual-minority youth and 40 percent of gender-minority youth who responded to the survey said they were satisfied with their lives, up from 42 and 35 percent two years earlier.

Headline: News
Full_Text: "I have asked my ministry to draw up a comprehensive picture of what we know about children who are sent abroad," Minister Anders Adlercreutz (SPP) said. Finland's Minister of Education, Anders Adlercreutz (SPP), said he wants to investigate whether girls are being taken out of the country to undergo female genital mutilation (FMG), and to see how common the practice might be. Earlier this week, Yle published an investigative story about some Somali parents living in Finland who have sent their children to disciplinary institutions in Somalia. Once there, according to the report, they are subjected to severe treatment — including physical abuse and being locked in chains. According to news agency STT, Minister Adlercreutz characterised the contents of Yle's report as extremely serious. "I have asked my ministry to draw up a comprehensive picture of what we know about children who are sent abroad - whether it is concerns so-called educational camps or, for example, genital mutilation of girls or women," he said, according to STT. Adlercreutz has previously said that it was known that children were being taken abroad for disciplinary reasons, but "we were not aware of such institutions". In 2024, Finland approved a law specifically banning the practice and preparation of FGM.

Headline: News
Full_Text: More than 66 percent of respondents said they would approve of a social media ban for youths under the age of 15. People in Finland are increasingly in favour of banning social media use for people under the age of 15, according to a recent survey. The poll, commissioned by price-tracking website firm Hintaopas in December, found 66.5 percent of respondents supporting a social media ban for under-15s. It said a survey about the topic last summer found 57.3 percent of respondents holding such an opinion, according to the company. The change reflects a nearly 10 percentage point increase in around six months. Support for a social media ban for youths increased the most among respondents between the ages of 18 and 24, as well as those 65 and up. Around 1,000 people took part in the survey. In December, Australia became the first country in the world to ban the use of social media for people under the age of 16, and the idea has gained popularity in other parts of the world. For example, Finnish Prime Minister Petteri Orpo (NCP) has identified social media as a major factor behind the lack of adequate amounts of physical activity among young people and children. Meanwhile, Finland's Institute for Health and Welfare (THL) and the National Agency for Education recently issued stricter guidelines for children’s use of digital gadgets, including the call for a ban on the use of social media or smartphones for kids under the age of 13.

Headline: News
Full_Text: For the past two years, scratchcard winnings have only been redeemable by the person who purchased the card. Finland's Interior Ministry is examining whether scratchcards might once again be allowed as gifts. The investigation will consider whether winnings from a scratchcard could be claimed by someone other than the person who purchased the card. At the start of 2024, scratchcards were brought under mandatory identification rules. Since then, recipients of gifted cards have been unable to redeem any prizes they potentially offer. Parliament approved a new Lotteries Act in December. At the same time, legislators included a statement urging the government to explore ways to permit scratchcards to be given as gifts. Christmastime is traditionally the biggest season for lottery scratch card sales in Finland.

Headline: News
Full_Text: Some had to pay to get jobs in Finland, while others had to hand over their wages to the boss. The Helsinki Police Department's human trafficking unit has completed preliminary investigations into two separate criminal cases, both involving suspected extortionate labour practices. In the first case, cleaners were allegedly forced to return most of their wages to the company's head. On payday, these full-time workers were required to hand back the bulk of their earnings to the suspect. "The complainants said they had little choice but to agree to the repayment of their wages," said lead investigator Nils Majewski. "Without work-based residence permits, they would have faced deportation from Finland." Police suspect that a man registered as an unemployed jobseeker was in fact working for the cleaning company officially owned by his spouse. In practice, though, he is alleged to have run the business despite holding no official position within the firm. Over three years, the man is thought to have drawn around 50,000 euros in social benefits. One of the victims is meanwhile estimated to have been deprived of roughly 130,000 euros in unpaid wages, police said. In the second case, an entrepreneur in the cleaning and restaurant sectors is suspected of luring workers from their home country and from outside the EU. Those recruited from the business owner's country of origin were relatives or acquaintances. Some workers were allegedly required to pay so-called "starting fees" to secure employment. "One employee paid around 6,500 euros," Majewski said, adding that the preliminary investigation suggests the entrepreneur also borrowed money from employees and failed to repay it. Workers did not receive their wages every month, or were paid too little. Police suspect the number of victims to be around twenty, with their unpaid wages totalling just under 200,000 euros. Both cases are now under consideration by prosecutors.

Headline: News
Full_Text: Around 50,000 more people were unemployed last month than in November 2024. More people were again out of work in November, according to the national number cruncher. Joblessness continued to rise in November, according to Statistics Finland. The trending unemployment rate climbed to 10.6 percent, up 0.2 percentage points from October. This marks the bleakest reading since 2009, when the agency began tracking the trending jobless rate. The trend tracking is a measure of long-term changes in employment and unemployment, eliminating the peaks and valleys of factors like seasonal employment variations. The agency reported that as of November, there were around 50,000 more unemployed people this year compared to the same month in 2024. In total, 276,000 people in Finland were out of work last month. The overall number of those in work changed little compared with last year. However, part-time employment increased, while full-time jobs continued to decline. Last week, the governement said Finland's economic recovery this year has been weaker than expected. According to the Finance Ministry, public finances may still need to be adjusted by 1.4 billion euros during this government term by some combination of tax hikes and budget cuts.

Headline: News
Full_Text: The votes fell 108-54, with 21 abstentions and 16 representatives absent. Finnish MPs on Friday approved a law that aims to lower the threshold to dismiss employees. The votes fell 108-54, with 21 abstentions and 16 representatives absent. After the law goes into effect, a "proper reason" will suffice for terminating an employment contract, compared to current law requiring both "proper and weighty" grounds. Earlier this month, Parliament's Employment and Equality Committee greenlit the government's plans to lower the threshold for employers to fire workers. At the time, the committee's chair, MP Arto Satonen (NCP), said the reform was especially aimed at improving the operating conditions of small and medium-sized companies — as they will be more willing to hire staff if the threshold for dismissal is lowered. Opposition parties often referred to the government-proposed legislation as a "firing law". Opposition MP Pia Hiltunen (SDP) strayed from her party's position in Friday's vote, siding with the government in favour of the legislation. According to news agency STT's information, the Social Democrats plan to reprimand the MP for doing so.

Headline: News
Full_Text: In 2001, Linda Lampenius was forced to buy an advertisement in Ilta-Sanomat to persuade the millionaire Peter Nygård, now a convicted sex offender, to drop his defamation claims. Sanoma Media Finland plans to reimburse violinist Linda Lampenius for the cost of a newspaper advertisement she was compelled to pay for more than 20 years ago to apologise to ex-fashion tycoon Peter Nygård, Suomen Kuvalehti reports. In 2001, Lampenius paid for a full-page ad in Ilta-Sanomat and gave an interview to halt the ex-fashion tycoon's demands for damages over alleged defamation. The dispute stemmed from comments she made in 1997 about an encounter with Nygård during a trip to California, in which she warned against sending young Finnish women to his residence. She told tabloid magazine 7 päivää that Nygård had shown her photographs of naked women taken at his villa. The advertisement cost 35,000 Finnish marks, which these days amounts to nearly 9,000 euros. Finnish-born Nygård was convicted in Canada in 2024 on multiple counts of sexual assault that took place between the 1980s and the mid-2000s. Sanoma's chief executive, Pia Kalsta, told Suomen Kuvalehti that the repayment would still need to be discussed with Lampenius.

Headline: News
Full_Text: Three 14-year-old girls were injured in the attack at a school in Pirkkala earlier this year. Prosecutors have filed three attempted murder charges against a 16-year-old boy over the school stabbing that took place in Pirkkala this past spring. Three 14-year-old girls were injured in the incident at Vähäjärvi School on 20 May. Police have previously said the boy selected the girls at random, and that neither he nor the victims — all pupils at the school — knew one another. After the stabbings, the boy left the school. Police arrested him shortly afterwards at a nearby square. The girls' injuries were not life-threatening, and they were discharged from the hospital the following day. The boy had published an online manifesto, saying he had planned the attack for half a year and wanted to do something "meaningful, exciting, and go to prison for two to four years". In August, the court ordered the boy to undergo a psychiatric evaluation. He remains in custody with the case set to be heard at Pirkanmaa district court on 19 December.

Headline: News
Full_Text: The move aims to make Finland more attractive to international students and returnees, while supporting those with limited Finnish or Swedish skills, the education ministry says. The Ministry of Education and Culture has announced that the first authorisations to offer general upper-secondary education in English have been granted. Approvals were given to Gradia — a Jyväskylä-based educational consortium — and institutions in the cities of Helsinki, Oulu, Pori, and Tampere, covering a total of five upper-secondary schools, a ministry press release explained on Monday. "The authorisation to provide education applies to Helsinki Upper Secondary School of Languages, Jyväskylän Lyseo Upper Secondary School, Oulun Lyseon lukio (upper secondary school), Porin lukio general upper secondary school and Pyynikin lukio upper secondary school (in Tampere)," the ministry said in the release. The English School in Helsinki already offers an English-language curriculum for upper secondary pupils. According to Education Minister Anders Adlercreutz (SPP), the move aims to make Finland more attractive to international students and returnees, while supporting those with limited Finnish or Swedish skills. The English upper-secondary courses are set to begin next August, with around 200 students expected to enrol in the programmes each year. The first English matriculation exams are set for autumn 2028. "The matriculation examination in English is intended for students whose language skills are too limited to be able to complete the general upper secondary education syllabus and the related matriculation examination in Finnish or Swedish," the release explained. "Matriculation candidates whose primary language is neither Finnish nor Swedish are required to pass a compulsory mother tongue and literature test in either Finnish or Swedish in the form of a second language and literature test," it continued. Amended note at 14:41 on 4 November 2025 to reflect that this item was edited shortly after publication for clarity and to name the specific schools. Edited at 10:17 on 5 November 2025 to add that the English School in Helsinki already offers an English-language curriculum.

Headline: News
Full_Text: These types of crimes increased significantly compared to 2024. Using various schemes, criminals swiped a total of around 70 million euros from victims in Finland in 2025, according to Finance Finland (FFI). FFI represents the financial interests of the country's financial sector. According to FFI, phishing scams were the most common method criminals used in bilking people out of their money, stealing around 22 million that way. In total, there were attempts to defraud people in the country of around 150 million euros last year. However, banks managed to claw back or block payments that were headed to the criminals, FFI noted. These types of crimes have increased significantly compared to 2024, when there were attempts to defraud people in Finland of around 107 million euros. That year, banks were able to retrieve or block around 40 percent of the payments. There are ways to avoid getting caught up in a scam, including:

Headline: News
Full_Text: The third-term opposition MP said she wants to leave politics because she is frustrated by the policies of the current government, which she describes as having features of "Trumpism". Member of Parliament Hanna Kosonen of the opposition Centre party has announced that she will step down from parliament at the end of this term, and also retire from politics. In an interview with Helsingin Sanomat, the Savonlinna MP said she is quitting politics because of her frustration with the current right-wing government — which she says displays features of "Trumpism". "This atmosphere, which has been created by all this scissors-clipping [referring to the government's austerity measures], certainly does not build trust or make economic growth possible," she told the daily. She also cited the current nature of public debate as another reason why she is stepping away from politics, noting that she does not want to become cynical, as she considers the work of an MP to be very meaningful. Kosonen is a third-term MP. She served as Minister of Science and Culture in 2019 and 2020, first under PM Antti Rinne (SDP) and then under his replacement, Sanna Marin.

Headline: News
Full_Text: Terno Hedman fatally shot his pregnant partner on a busy street in the centre of Tampere in front of the couple's child. Turku Court of Appeal has upheld the life imprisonment sentence handed down to Terno Alkki Rikhard Hedman for the shooting to death of his pregnant partner in the centre of Tampere in September 2024. Pirkanmaa District Court found Hedman guilty of murder at the original trial in February last year. He was also convicted of a string of other offences, including two counts of assault, aggravated assault, public endangerment, a firearms infraction, violent resistance, and drug use. In its ruling, the appeal court agreed with the district court's verdict that the killing was premeditated and also presented a serious danger to the public. In addition, the appeal court found that the killing was also carried out in a particularly brutal manner. The victim was pregnant with Hedman's child at the time, and their other child, 4 years old at the time, witnessed the killing. Although the murder conviction was upheld, the court however dismissed the charges of aggravated assault and attempted aggravated assault. These charges related to two bystanders on the street, who were also injured by the bullets Hedman fired. In the view of the court of appeal, Hedman could not have reasonably foreseen that the bullets intended for the victim would also hit the bystanders. The appeal court's decision is not final, meaning it can be further appealed to Finland's Supreme Court. During the first trial, Hedman told the victim's family in court that he would accept the verdict and would not appeal. He changed his mind however and appealed the verdict of murder. Both Hedman and his victim are members of the Romani community. Yle includes their backgrounds in the reporting of the case because of the ongoing societal discussion about serious acts of violence within Finland's Roma community.

Headline: News
Full_Text: Estonians are the largest foreign group incarcerated in Finland. Finland and Estonia are moving to streamline the transfer of prisoners between the two countries. Justice Minister Leena Meri (Finns) and Estonia's Minister of Justice and Digital Affairs, Liisa-Ly Pakosta, signed a joint declaration to that effect in Tallinn on Tuesday. Estonians make up the largest group of foreign inmates in Finnish prisons, according to Finland's justice ministry. The agreement aims to identify obstacles to prisoner transfers and to strengthen cooperation between the two countries' prison authorities. As part of the effort, Estonia plans to amend its legislation to remove a provision under which it has not accepted Estonian prisoners with fewer than six months remaining on their sentences. The share of foreign inmates has been rising in recent years, growing to just over 20 percent in 2024, according to the Prison and Probation Service of Finland (Rise). Last year, the group reported that Finnish prisons had exceeded capacity.

Headline: News
Full_Text: A flagpole was broken, a flag ripped and graffiti was painted on a wall of the building in the upscale Kulosaari neighbourhood. Helsinki police are investigating an incident at the Iranian embassy in the western Kulosaari district. The police suspect that at least two people entered the embassy grounds on Monday. Authorities were called to the embassy around 5pm, but the suspects had fled the scene by the time they arrived. According to a police statement, the individuals broke a flagpole, ripped the Iranian flag and defaced an exterior wall with paint. The suspects left in a car, which police later spotted in Itäkeskus, eastern Helsinki. Police detained two male suspects who were in the vehicle. The incident is being investigated as aggravated vandalism and breach of public peace. After questioning the suspects, the police will decide on whether to they will be formally placed under arrest. The police are also investigating the identities of other individuals who entered the embassy grounds. The incident came as Iranian authorities have a launched a deadly crackdown on anti-government protests in the country. On Tuesday, Foreign Minister Elina Valtonen (NCP) summoned Iranian Ambassador Javad Aghazadeh Khoei to express concern over an internet blackout imposed by Iranian authorities and the violent suppression of protests. More than 600 people have been killed and thousands detained, human rights groups said on Tuesday. There are currently 91 Finns in Iran who have filed travel declarations with the Finnish Foreign Ministry, Finland's Ambassador-at-large for the Middle East and the Persian Gulf, Harri Kämäräinen, told Yle on Tuesday morning. "Presumably most of them are dual citizens, Finns who may have gone to spend the Christmas holidays with relatives in Iran. Contact has been made with all of them," Kämäräinen said, adding that the actual number of Finns in Iran may be higher. According to Kämäräinen, the Finnish embassy in the Iranian capital, Tehran, is maintaining nearly normal operations despite the unrest. He is the former Finnish Ambassador to Iran. On Monday, the embassy warned that arbitrary arrests of foreigners were on the rise in Iran. According to Statistics Finland, there were more than 12,000 Iranian-born people living in Finland in 2024.

Headline: News
Full_Text: Investigators believe two individuals provided false information about costs and the quality of construction as they applied for state-subsidised loans. Police suspect two individuals linked to the construction company Sisco of aggravated subsidy fraud. According to investigators, the accused defrauded the state of millions of euros. The case is centred on guarantee and subsidy loan applications at the Housing Finance and Development Centre of Finland (Ara) in 2014-2017 — intended for state-funded housing projects. Police suspect the individuals of providing false information about construction costs and the quality of construction as they applied for the loans. According to a statement issued by prosecutors, Ara granted the company a total of around 54 million euros in loans. It said Ara suffered estimated damages of at least around 15 million euros. The suspects have denied any wrongdoing.

Headline: News
Full_Text: Finnish and Estonian authorities suspect the Fitburg was involved in deliberately damaging an underwater cable in the Baltic Sea on New Year's Eve. Finnish authorities have lifted the seizure order on the Fitburg cargo vessel, which is suspected of damaging an undersea cable in the Gulf of Finland on New Year's Eve. In a statement released on Monday, the Finnish Border Guard said the ship was escorted out of Finland's territorial waters from Kantvik port in Kirkkonummi at around 11am. Risto Lohi, who is leading the National Bureau of Investigation's (NBI) preliminary probe into the incident, said that both Finnish and Estonian police have completed their investigations, which is why the seizure could be lifted. "Helsinki District Court yesterday, Sunday, detained a crew member of the Fitburg vessel in a new hearing. Some of the crew remain under a travel ban," Lohi added. Last week, Finnish police applied to remand one crew member in custody, which the court granted on Sunday, while three others have been placed under a travel ban. The reasons for the suspect to be further detained were also upgraded from reasonable suspicion to probable cause. Fitchburg's crew consisted of a total of 14 members — who are citizens of Russia, Georgia, Kazakhstan, and Azerbaijan — and it sailed under the flag of Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. Finnish authorities took control of the vessel on New Year's Eve in the Gulf of Finland amid suspicions that the ship, which was en route from Russia to Israel, deliberately damaged a telecommunications cable by dragging its anchor along the seabed. The incident is being investigated as suspected aggravated criminal damage, suspected attempted aggravated criminal damage, and suspected aggravated interference with telecommunications. There have been a spate of similar incidents in the Baltic Sea in recent years, in which vessels are suspected of deliberately damaging underwater cables. Yle News reporter Matt Schilke compiled this report last week on the phenomenon.

Headline: News
Full_Text: A group of middle schoolers and their teacher were injured in the fall after the temporary bridge gave way in May 2023. Western Uusimaa District Court has handed down a suspended prison term of five months to the project manager of a scaffolding firm after finding him guilty on 19 counts of aggravated negligent injury. The charges relate to the collapse of a temporary metal and plywood bridge in the Tapiola district of Espoo in May 2023. The bridge gave way as a total of 44 pedestrians were attempting to cross. The collapse led to a group of middle school teenagers suffering a range of injuries after they plunged about five metres to the ground. In its verdict on Friday, the court ruled that the defendant, aged in his late 30s, neglected his duties by approving the use of the temporary bridge, which was ordered by the City of Espoo to provide a route across Itätuulenkuja while construction work was ongoing. This approval was given although the load-bearing capacity of the bridge had not been verified in the assembly work designed and supervised by the defendant. The court noted that the bridge was assembled from parts made by different scaffolding manufacturers and did not match standard structures. Ensuring the bridge's durability was the project manager's responsibility, the verdict added. Charges against a second defendant, a supervisor with the construction company that built the bridge, were dismissed by the court on Friday. Police initially suspected eight people of crimes in relation to the incident, but the charges against six of the eight were dropped before the case came to court. The City of Espoo also avoided any charges arising from the bridge collapse. The group of middle school students, numbering about 23, as well as their teacher, suffered injuries ranging from minor to very serious as a result of the fall. Six of the teenage victims were left with permanent impairments, according to Finland's Safety Investigation Authority. All of the injured were eighth-grade students from Helsinki's Kalasatama School.

Headline: News
Full_Text: The men were tasked with retrieving the drugs from a shipping container and hiding them in nearby woods. Helsinki District Court has sentenced two Albanian men in their 30s to prison terms of around eight years for aggravated drug offences. The court found that the men had been involved in smuggling around 45 kilograms of cocaine into Finland from Ecuador in a shipping container. The haul, which could have fetched 4.5 million euros on the street, was intercepted by Finnish Customs. After arriving in Finland on 15 September, 2025 and scouting the harbour, the men returned five days later at night in a rowboat they had found nearby. At the port, they found the shipping container and cocaine, which had been hidden inside the container's refrigeration unit. According to the men, they had each been promised 10,000 euros in their home country for travelling to Finland, retrieving the drugs, and hiding them in the forest. Someone else was to take the stash from there. The district court's verdict can still be appealed. In a similar case, the district court recently sentenced two Swedish men to nearly eight years in prison. They had received a 44-kilo shipment of cocaine smuggled from Colombia at Vuosaari Harbour last May.

Headline: News
Full_Text: The 16-year-old boy stabbed three 14-year-old girls at the  Vähäjärvi School in Pirkkala in May. The Pirkanmaa District Court on Wednesday convicted a 16-year-old male of three counts of attempted murder in connection with the school stabbings in Pirkkala this past spring. However, a psychiatric evaluation carried out previously found that the teen was not criminally responsible, meaning he did not understand his actions or their consequences. Public health authority THL has ordered him into involuntary psychiatric treatment. As a result, the defendant was not sentenced to punishment. He was, however, ordered to pay some 39,600 euros to the three victims. According to police, before the attack, the boy carried out hundreds of searches using artificial intelligence, including queries about stabbing the neck and heart, and about human anatomy. He also searched for information on mass killings, school shootings, police procedures, concealing evidence, manifestos, and how to commit crimes. In addition, he wrote a manifesto in Finnish and English, saying that his motive was a desire to do something significant and to bring excitement into his life. He also said he wanted to be sent to prison for two to four years.

Headline: News
Full_Text: Helsinki District Court imposed an enhanced travel ban on all three suspects. They are still under investigation by the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI). Helsinki District Court has released three men suspected of financing a terrorist group. Two of the suspects were released last Friday and the third on Tuesday this week. However, the District Court has imposed an enhanced travel ban on the men, who are aged 47, 57 and 58. That usually means monitoring with electronic ankle bracelets and required periods of time when the suspect must remain home. Last month, the district court remanded the men on suspicion of financing a terrorist group. According to Yle sources, the men are suspected of having provided financial support to the Kurdistan Workers' Party (PKK). The PKK is an armed group that has sought self-rule for the Kurds. It has been designated as a terrorist organisation by the EU, the US, Turkey and others. Last May, the PKK said that it had disbanded. During Finland’s Nato accession process, Turkey repeatedly demanded that Finland hand over individuals that Ankara suspected of PKK involvement. In late 2022, Helsinki police banned the display of flags representing the PKK and related organisations. According to the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI), the suspected crimes began in Helsinki in 2023 and continued until early November this year. The District Court's remand decisions were based crimes suspected to have occurred in early November. The 58-year-old suspect is registered as a resident of Imatra, while the 47-year-old’s address is in Sipoo. The 57-year-old’s address is unknown. According to Helsingin Sanomat, the men are of Kurdish origin. The NBI is still continuing to investigate the suspected terrorist crimes. It says that the preliminary investigation has been ongoing since the beginning of the year. The head of the investigation, Senior Detective Superintendent Mikko Laaksonen, declined to comment on any details of the investigation to Yle. The men were detained during a late-night traffic stop in Ruokolahti, South Karelia, in early November. Around the same time, the Kurdish Democratic Society Centre (NCDK Finland) said that police had raided its community centre in eastern Helsinki. The NBI froze their assets in mid-December, except for funds for essential expenses such as food, housing and healthcare.

Headline: News
Full_Text: The case dealt with one of the biggest drug smuggling operations Finland has ever seen. Helsinki's Court of Appeal on Tuesday handed down new verdicts in a drug case related to the Swedish criminal gang Dödspatrullen. The appeal court reviewed the case of 12 of the defendants in the sprawling case heard last year by the city's district court. The higher court increased the prison terms of five of the defendants found guilty of aggravated drug crimes to a sentence of up to 13 years. The court also extended the sentences of two other defendants. Deviating from the district court's decision, the appeal court found that seven of the defendants had committed several crimes, particularly for importing the drugs. The district court convicted 10 defendants of single counts of aggravated drug offenses, and convicted two defendants of aggravated money laundering. The lower court handed most of those defendants 10-year prison terms. The case dealt with one of the biggest drug smuggling operations Finland has ever seen.

Headline: News
Full_Text: Police were trying to clear away environmental protesters from a busy street at rush hour in downtown Helsinki on an October afternoon more than five years ago. The Helsinki Court of Appeal has fined three city police officers for pepper spraying demonstrators at an environmental protest in the capital on 3 October 2020. The officers were trying to clear away the Elokapina (Extinction Rebellion) protesters blocking a busy thoroughfare in the Kaisaniemi district during rush hour. Some of the protesters had locked themselves together and onto objects they had taken to the demonstration. Police officers initially tried other methods of removing the protesters, but managed to clear the area after deploying the pepper spray. The appeal court upheld the district court's decision to fine the leading officer for approving the use of pepper spray. The appeal court's decision also found two other officers guilty of negligent breach of duty in the case. The appeal court found that while the officer in charge had ordered the use of pepper spray, it said the other officers had the opportunity — and obligation — to independently consider whether the situation called for using pepper spray. The appeal court fined all three of the officers, but otherwise did not change the district court's decision. In the district court trial, the prosecutor had initially demanded that seven officers should face penalties for their involvement in the incident. However, the district court dismissed the charges against four of the officers.

Headline: News
Full_Text: Australian police suspect that Sunday's mass shooting was a targeted antisemitic attack. Following a deadly shooting attack on attendees at a Hanukkah event in Sydney, Australia over the weekend, the Helsinki Police Department has raised the security alert level in the capital. Australia saw its worst mass shooting in nearly three decades on Sunday by Sydney's famous Bondi Beach. According to local police, a father-and-son duo opened fire on people attending the Jewish event, described by officials as a targeted antisemitic attack. More than 1,000 people were taking part in the event at the time. As of Monday, the Australian attack's death toll stood at 15, according to news agency Reuters, citing local authorities. While authorities in Helsinki confirmed that the police department has raised its preparedness level, they did not offer details about those efforts. "We have taken note of the events [in Australia] and raised our alert level," Helsinki Police Chief Inspector Jari Kaikko said. Police in Stockholm, Sweden, have raised security details at synagogues and Jewish schools, according to the country's public broadcaster, SVT. "I don't want to go into details, but this is exactly the type of activity in question," Kaikko said. Police in Turku have also raised security levels in the southwestern city. According to an Yle journalist in Turku, officers were seen in an unmarked police car parked by the city's synagogue. "This is a sad event, and even though it happened on the other side of the world, information about things like this spreads like wildfire," Kaikko said.

Headline: News
Full_Text: The former rapper spent about eight years in Finland, during which time he accumulated an extensive record of violent crimes. Ex-rapper and convicted rapist Milan Jaff has been deported from Finland, the tabloid Iltalehti reported on Friday evening. He was flown back to Iraq on Monday night. Chief Inspector Simo Kauppinen, Head of the Aliens Affairs Unit of the Helsinki Police, confirmed to Yle that a return flight to Iraq left Finland that night. He said it was a joint Nordic return flight carrying several people from different countries who had been issued deportation orders, but declined to reveal the identity of anyone on board. "The flight arrived successfully," Kauppinen said. The Finnish Immigration Service (Migri) ordered Jaff to be deported from Finland in September. Jaff was also indefinitely banned from entering the entire 29-nation Schengen area and the 27 member states of the European Union. Jaff spent about eight years in Finland, during which time he accumulated an extensive criminal record. He arrived in the country in 2017 as a minor. Two years later, he was convicted of robbery, home invasion and other offences. In 2022, the Helsinki District Court sentenced Jaff, then aged 22, to 10 years in prison for a string of violent and drug crimes. The court declared that Jaff was the leader of an organised criminal group known as the Kurdish Mafia. His rap sheet includes assault, rape and attempted murder. While in prison, he was the victim of serious assault in 2023. Jaff was released from prison in August but immediately taken back into custody.

Headline: News
Full_Text: The former Finns Party politician was recently found guilty of assault, making unlawful threats and various firearms offences in relation to a late-night incident at a karaoke bar in April 2024. Member of Parliament Timo Vornanen has resigned from his position as a senior constable with the Eastern Finland Police Department. Vornanen had taken leave from the force when he was elected to parliament in spring 2023. In a Facebook post, the politician explained that he made the decision to quit after his lawyer informed him the department was preparing to dismiss him. "Now, at this point, after all these years, I feel it is better to leave the organisation on my own initiative rather than through dismissal," Vornanen wrote in the post, referrring to the 30 years he had served on the force. The resignation comes into effect from 1 January 2026. Helsinki District Court found Vornanen guilty last week of assault, making unlawful threats and various firearms offences in relation to a late-night incident outside a karaoke bar in April 2024. He was handed an eight-month suspended prison sentence and also ordered to pay 17,000 euros in compensation. He was ejected from the Finns Party in the aftermath of the incident, but he remains in parliament as an independent. Vornanen has indicated his intention to appeal the court's verdict.

Headline: News
Full_Text: Benefits agency Kela and the Finnish Tax Administration also have plans to switch to US-based cloud storage. Finland's Ministry of Justice is considering halting its plans to start using US-hosted cloud services, according to news group Uutissuomalainen (USU). The reason is the changing geopolitical situation. Given the increasingly uncertain relationship with the US, some European countries have started to wonder whether relying on US technology providers is a good idea. For example, it was reported this week that France plans to stop using US-based Microsoft Teams and Zoom apps for video conferencing, replacing them with a domestically developed platform. According to EuroNews, the move is part of France's strategy to stop using foreign tech vendors — especially ones from the United States. Finnish MEP Aura Salla (NCP) has warned of risks that if it decided to, the US has the ability to cut Europe off from American web services, according to Svenska Yle, the public broadcaster's Swedish-language news outlet. Earlier this week, Salla, who was formerly Meta's Public Policy Director and Head of EU Affairs, issued a press release warning about such risks. It was published by the news agency STT. Besides the justice ministry, benefits agency Kela and the Finnish Tax Administration also plan to use US-based cloud storage. In an Yle article published on Monday, Finnish cybersecurity expert Petteri Järvinen lamented that Europe has left its information systems at the mercy of American companies. The Ministry of Justice has been planning to shift all of its data concerning candidates, voters and vote counting to US-based Amazon Web Services. The ministry is due to make a final decision about the matter in the spring, according to USU.

Headline: News
Full_Text: Finnish prosecutors have filed charges against a US citizen over his suspected involvement in the extortion of patients at the Vastaamo psychotherapy centre. Less than a week after hacker Aleksanteri Kivimäki was released by the Helsinki Court of Appeal, prosecutors have filed new charges in the Vastaamo psychotherapy centre case. The Prosecutor's Office says the new suspect is a 28-year-old foreign national. Swedish-language broadcaster Svenska Yle reports that he is an American living in Estonia. He has been charged with aiding an attempted aggravated extortion. Patients received emails demanding payment in cryptocurrency to prevent their medical records from being leaked online. Police linked him to the case by tracing bitcoins. In a sting operation, the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) followed the payments and found that some went to an account held by Kivimäki, and some to an account the suspect could access. According to the prosecutor's statement, the attempted aggravated extortion took place between 28 September and 23 October 2020. The suspect denies the charges. After a lengthy trial at Helsinki District Court, Kivimäki was handed a six-year and three-month prison sentence in April 2024 for charges related to the hacking of psychotherapy centre Vastaamo's patient database Kivimäki was convicted of an aggravated data breach offence, nearly 9,600 counts of aggravated invasion of privacy related to the dissemination of information, more than 21,300 counts of attempted aggravated extortion and 20 counts of aggravated blackmail.

Headline: News
Full_Text: Grok is an AI chatbot developed by Musk's company xAI. Tech billionaire Elon Musk shared a post on social media platform X earlier this week, which claimed that his company's AI chatbot Grok was the number one most downloaded app in Finland. The claim was initially posted by the 'Tesla Owners Silicon Valley' account, and re-posted by Musk to his 223 million followers. Musk added that Grok "might have a shot of #1 app worldwide this week" to his post. However, the app itself denied the claim that it was the most downloaded in Finland — noting that the top positions in Finland's download charts are held by Vinted, Dott and Chat GPT. When asked for further explanation, the chatbot responded that the claim may have been a "humorous exaggeration". Grok is an AI chatbot developed by xAI, Musk's own AI company. According to news agency Reuters, the company plans to open source Grok version 2 next week.

Headline: News
Full_Text: Military officials from Germany and the Netherlands have also since departed Greenland. Two Finnish liaison officers have concluded their fact-finding mission in Greenland, according to information obtained by Yle. Yle's source said that the officers would be heading back to Finland by the end of this week. Finland sent the officers to Greenland last week, following a request from Denmark to carry out a multinational military mission in the region. Denmark made the move as US President Donald Trump's threats to annex Greenland continued to escalate. Apart from Finland, the countries sending military personnel to Greenland included France, Germany, Sweden, Norway, the Netherlands and the UK. The US was also invited to take part. So far, military officials from Germany and the Netherlands have since departed Greenland. Trump has repeatedly claimed the US needs to seize control of the semiautonomous island because it does not believe Denmark, which holds the territory, is capable of defending it. Denmark and Greenland began negotiations with the United States about 10 days ago, but the exact content of those talks has not been made public. As Finland announced that it was sending two officers to the region, Defence Minister Antti Häkkänen (NCP) said the move was not a message to members in the Nato military alliance, but rather a broader announcement to the world regarding European allies' commitment to security in the Arctic. The move appeared to frustrate Trump, and he threatened punitive tariffs on the participating countries. However, on Wednesday, the American president said that he was calling off the threatened tariffs. In another reversal, Trump has also said that the US will not follow through on his perceived threats that the US could take Greenland by force. After meeting with Nato's Secretary General, Mark Rutte, Trump announced on his social media channel Truth Social that he and Rutte had "formed the framework of a future deal with respect to Greenland" — as well as the Arctic region.

Headline: News
Full_Text: The body does not include Palestinian representatives, while Israel says it has not approved the council proposed by Donald Trump. Finnish president Alexander Stubb has been invited to join what Donald Trump calls an executive board for Gaza, according to the Finnish president's office. The news arrived shortly after Trump said Finland was among the countries facing possible new export levies to the United States. The board is meant to implement Trump's proposed peace plan between Israel and Gaza and to oversee the territory's reconstruction. Russia said on Monday that President Vladimir Putin had also been invited to the group. Palestinians, however, are not represented on the council, and Israel has stated that it has not approved the body proposed by Trump. The council's creation forms part of the ceasefire agreement between Israel and Hamas. The United States announced last week that the truce had entered its second phase. Among those named to the new administrative body are US secretary of state Marco Rubio, special envoy Steve Witkoff, Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, former UK prime minister Tony Blair, and several businessmen. Helsingin Sanomat was the first to report the news of Stubb's invitation.

Headline: News
Full_Text: The wreck's tanks contain around 100,000 litres of light fuel oil. Experts from the Finnish Border Guard and the Finnish Heritage Agency are examining the wreck of the Finnish ship Ilmarinen — which sank in 1941 — for a possible oil recovery operation, the Finnish Environment Institute reported. The wreck's tanks, which are sitting at the bottom of the Baltic Sea, are estimated to contain around 100,000 litres of light fuel oil. If the operation is decided upon, it will be put out to tender and carried out during 2024. The coastal defence ship Ilmarinen was active during the Winter and Continuation Wars. It struck a mine in 1941, sinking with a loss of 271 sailors' lives. The wreck lies partially sunk in the mud at a depth of about 80 metres. The Ilmarinen was the flagship of the Finnish Navy from 1933 until its sinking in 1941. The wreck was found in 1990. The wreck site is classified as a war grave, which has been taken into account for the preliminary study and any subsequent oil recovery operation. Last week, investigators pulled the bow ramp of the passenger ferry MS Estonia from its wreck, which is roughly 15 km from the site of the Ilmarinen wreck.

Headline: News
Full_Text: The average age of veterans who served in Finland's wars is 97. The association for frontline veterans said it was staging its final meeting on Saturday, when it will terminate operations. The association's chair, Matti Louekoski, said the advanced age of its members contributed to operations coming to an end. Today with an average age of 97, veterans are generally unable to participate in the group's meetings and other organisational activities. The Tammenlehvä Heritage Association will now take over veteran advocacy and matters related to preserving the legacy of Finnish veterans. In 2020, the Finnish War Veterans Federation said the majority of surviving veterans were now female, with Finland's last vet expected to survive until 2036.
